ch07.note: Kuroda Yoshitaka (1546–1604), better known by his courtesy name Kanbei and, in his later years, by his monastic name Josui, was Hideyoshi’s ablest strategist and the mind behind many of his campaigns. Gotō Matabei, who bargains with the old gunsmith here, was a retainer of the Kuroda house. (Printed folio 418.)

ch07.anchor: Listening, Gotō Matabei was won over root and branch
ch07.note: Gotō Mototsugu (1560–1615), called Matabei, a retainer of the Kuroda and one of the most celebrated fighting men of his day. He later broke with the Kuroda, and died sword in hand for the losing Toyotomi cause at the fall of Ōsaka in 1615—so that the officer here won over by a gunsmith’s single-minded devotion ended as a byword for reckless valor. (Printed folio 420.)

ch07.anchor: famous in the histories as the Taiko kenchi
ch07.note: The Taikō kenchi, Hideyoshi’s cadastral survey, carried out piece by piece across the country from the 1580s on. It measured every field by a standard rod, rated its yield in koku of rice, set one registered cultivator against each plot, and fixed the tax on that footing. It swept away the old tangle of overlapping rights and gave the new regime a firm grip on the land and its people; historians count it, with the sword-hunt, one of the twin foundations of the early-modern order. Taikō is the honorific of a retired regent, Hideyoshi’s own later title. (Printed folio 425.)

ch07.anchor: became Kanpaku himself in his place
ch07.note: The kanpaku was the imperial regent, highest of all court offices, held for centuries only by the Fujiwara nobility. That Hideyoshi, born a peasant, should hold it was without precedent; he contrived it in 1585 by having himself adopted into the noble Konoe house, and put out the sitting regent, Nijō Akizane, to take the post. From it comes his familiar title Taikō, borne by a kanpaku who has passed the office on. (Printed folio 450.)

ch07.anchor: until he entered his final meditation in Jōwa 2, the year 835
ch07.note: By Shingon belief, Kōbō Daishi did not die in 835 but entered nyūjō, a deathless meditation, and sits to this day in his tomb at the Oku-no-in of Mount Kōya, his body incorrupt, awaiting the coming of the future Buddha Miroku; monks still carry meals to him. See the earlier note on Kōbō Daishi. (Printed folio 438.)

ch07.anchor: the Kanpaku Hidetsugu, would be made to take his own life
ch07.note: Toyotomi Hidetsugu (1568–1595), Hideyoshi’s nephew, adopted as his heir and made kanpaku in 1591. When Hideyoshi’s own son Hideyori was born, Hidetsugu became an obstacle; in 1595 he was sent up to Mount Kōya and ordered to cut himself open, and his women and children—some thirty of them—were then put to death in Kyoto. The novel calls him Hideyoshi’s “son” (he was the adopted heir) and dates the death eleven years from Tenshō 13, that is 1596; it fell in fact in 1595. (Printed folio 442.)

ch07.anchor: who quietly kidnapped women and sold them off overseas
ch07.note: The trade was real. Through the sixteenth century Japanese—many of them women, and captives taken in war—were bought up and shipped abroad, to Macao, to Manila in the Spanish Philippines, and beyond, the traffic riding on the back of the Nanban trade. Hideyoshi himself denounced it in the edict of 1587 by which he ordered the missionaries out of Japan. The kidnapping case of Tenshō 7 (1579) recorded here dramatizes a documented abuse. For Luzon, see the earlier note. (Printed folio 455.)

The concubine known as Kaga-dono was in fact Maa-hime (摩阿姫), a daughter of Maeda Toshiie, lord of Kaga. The novel gives her the name Gō-hime (豪姫), which properly belonged to another of Toshiie’s daughters—the one Hideyoshi and Nene adopted and married to Ukita Hideie—so that the two sisters are here run together. The pet name Maa, the title Kaga-dono, and the standing among Hideyoshi’s women all belong to the real concubine. Her earlier days as a hostage at Kita-no-shō are told in Chapter 4. (Printed folio 453.)

ch07.anchor: Mokujiki Ōgo had once been of the Sasaki clan of Ōmi
ch07.note: Mokujiki Ōgo (1536–1608), the monk who talked Mount Kōya out of destruction. It was his embassy that won Hideyoshi’s pardon for the mountain, and he went on to rebuild and reform it and to stand high in Hideyoshi’s favor. Mokujiki, “tree-eater,” is the name for an ascetic who forswears grain and cooked food, living on nuts and roots. (Printed folio 445.)

ch07.anchor: Deal with it as we did at Takamatsu Castle!
ch07.note: Hideyoshi’s flooding of Bicchū Takamatsu in 1582—he threw up a great dike and turned the river in to drown the castle—is among the most famous sieges of the age. It was there, mid-siege, that word reached him of Nobunaga’s murder at the Honnō-ji, whereupon he made terms in haste and marched his army back at astonishing speed to avenge his lord. At Ōta Castle here he turns the same tactic on the peasants. (Printed folio 427.)

ch07.anchor: There survives a famous letter that Nobunaga sent to Nene
ch07.note: This letter survives, and is one of the best-loved documents of the century: warm, teasing, and unexpectedly tender from so hard a man, with Nobunaga taking the wife’s part against the husband and calling Hideyoshi, to her face, his “bald rat” (hage-nezumi). The author gives it here in modern paraphrase; the wording is his, the substance the original’s. (Printed folio 451.)

The names are loanwords that came in with the goods: birōdo, velvet, from the Portuguese veludo; rasha, a fine wool broadcloth, from raxa; mōru, a braid of gold or silver thread; kaneken, a plain cotton or calico, from canequim; and sarasa, printed cotton or chintz. They mark the new wares of the Nanban trade passing through Sakai. (Printed folio 454.)
